app.title: Lunar Nav Kids — help Lumi land on the Moon

home.title: Help Lumi land on the Moon!
home.lead: At the bottom of the Moon, the Sun rolls along the hills and Earth plays hide-and-seek. Pick a good spot so Lumi has sunlight and can call home.
home.hello: Hi! I’m Lumi. I run on sunshine!
home.mascotLabel: Lumi, a friendly astronaut robot, waving
home.phasesNote: Three phases, three missions each. Your stars stay only on this device.
home.locked: Finish the {prev} phase to open it.

shackleton_ridge.name: Shackleton ridge
shackleton_ridge.desc: A high ridge on the edge of a giant crater

malapert_m1.name: Malapert Mountain
malapert_m1.desc: A big mountain with deep shadows

m1.title: Find the sunniest spot
m1.teaser: Where does the Sun shine longest?
m1.intro: Lumi needs sunshine for power. Watch the Sun roll along the real mountains for 30 days, from 1 July 2030.
m1.tag: The Sun never climbs high here. One small hill can hide it!
m1.sceneLabel: The sky all around {site} on day {day}, with the Sun and the real mountains
m1.mountains: The Sun is hiding behind the hills.
m1.below: The Sun is below the horizon.
m1.soFar: Sunny days so far: about {n} of {d}.
m1.stripLabel: The 30 days: yellow when the Sun shines (about {n} days in all)
m1.tip: On Shackleton ridge, walking just 300 m (three football fields) can turn {a} sunny days into about {x} to {y}.
m1.goals: Stars: look at two spots · look at all three · follow a spot to the end of July.

m2.title: When can we call home?
m2.intro: To call home, Earth must be above the hills, and a big antenna on Earth must see the Moon. Earth bobs up and down in the sky, so sometimes it hides.

badge.antennas: Earth is up, but no antenna can hear yet…
badge.mountains: Earth is hiding behind the hills…
badge.below: Earth is hiding below the horizon…

m2.sceneLabel: Earth in the sky of {site} on day {day}, with the real mountains
m2.wobble: Earth wobbles between {lo}° and {hi}° (this is called libration).
m2.whoText: Three giant antennas on Earth take turns listening, so almost always at least one can see the Moon.
m2.stripLabel: The 30 days: blue when Earth is in the sky (about {n} days in all)
m2.earthInSky: Earth in the sky: about {n} days
m2.hiding: Earth hiding: up to about {n} days in a row
m2.hidingAtLeast: Earth hiding: more than {n} days in a row
m2.callDays: You can call home on about {n} of the 30 days.
m2.why: The south pole is at the edge of the side of the Moon that faces Earth, so Earth sits low in the sky and a small wobble can hide it.
m2.goals: Stars: find a moment to call home · find Earth hiding · look at all three spots.

m3.title: Charge for the long night
m3.teaser: A Moon night lasts two weeks!
m3.intro: On Earth, night lasts a few hours. On {site}, a Moon night lasts {len}! Lumi must save enough energy to stay warm until sunrise.
m3.dayText: Sunlight charges the battery all the way up.
m3.nightText: No sunlight now. The battery keeps Lumi warm with {load} W until sunrise.
m3.ranOut: Oh no! The small battery ran out in the middle of the night. Lumi gets too cold!
m3.madeIt: Made it! The Sun is back and the battery still has 20 % — just right.
m3.phones: Lumi needs about as much energy as {n} phone batteries!
m3.sizeGrownups: That’s a battery of about {kwh} kWh, about as heavy as two grown-ups (about {kg} kg).
m3.size: That’s a battery of about {kwh} kWh, about {kg} kg.
m3.sizeAtLeast: That’s a battery of at least {kwh} kWh, at least {kg} kg.
m3.sizeTiny: Here the night is short, so a small battery (less than 1 kWh) is enough.
m3.rule: How we count: battery = {load} W × the longest night ÷ 0.8 (we only use {dod} % of it). A phone battery holds about {wh} Wh.
m3.goals: Stars: get through the night · watch a half-size battery run out · look at all three spots.

scene.taller: The mountains are drawn {n}× taller so you can see them.
scene.sunBigger: The Sun is drawn bigger, too.

questions.q: Which spot had the most sunshine in July 2030?
questions.why: {sunniest} is a high ridge, so the Sun shines there almost all the time.

questions.q: How does the Sun move in the sky at the Moon’s south pole?
options: It climbs high over our heads
It rolls around the sky, staying low
questions.why: At the pole the Sun stays just above the hills and goes all the way around.

questions.q: What do we need to call home from the Moon?
options: Earth above the hills, and a big antenna on Earth that sees the Moon
questions.why: Both are needed at the same time.

questions.q: At Mons Mouton (IM-2), how long is the longest night?
questions.why: The night there lasts about {night} days.

questions.q: Why does a Moon battery need to be big?
options: To keep Lumi warm through the whole long night
questions.why: With no sunlight, the battery must give power until the Sun comes back.

m4.title: The landing slipped!
m4.intro: Back to Mons Mouton (IM-2). Lumi was going to land on 1 July 2030, but the launch slipped to 11 July. Does the date matter?
m4.goals: Stars: try 1 July · try 11 July · pick the better date.
m4.stripLabel: The 30 days after landing on {date}: yellow when the Sun shines
m4.stripNote: The strip starts on the landing day.
m4.lumiDark: Brrr! We land in the dark. The Sun rises after about {n} days.
m4.lumiSun: Yay! We land in sunshine, with about {n} days of light before the night.
m4.question: Which date is better for Lumi?
m4.why: On 11 July Lumi lands in sunshine, with about {n} days of light before the first night. On 1 July it lands in the dark.

m5.title: Hit the target
m5.intro: Aim at the Shackleton ridge and land Lumi. Watch out: real landings can miss by hundreds of metres!
m5.goals: Stars: 1 for any landing, 2 for 15 or more sunny days, 3 for 22 or more.
m5.help: Arrow keys move the yellow aim; Enter lands. Or tap a square, then press Land.
m5.mapLabel: Landing map around the Shackleton ridge, 1 km wide, squares of 100 m
m5.stars1: 1 star. Fewer than 15 sunny days here. Try again!
m5.stars3: 3 stars! At least 22 sunny days. Great spot!
m5.none: Aim and land to see how many sunny days Lumi gets.
m5.miss: Here Lumi lands up to 200 m from where you aim, like a real lander can.
m5.range: 8 out of 10 spots within 300 m of the target get about {x} to {y} sunny days.
m5.legend: Colours: dark blue = no Sun in July 2030; lilac to yellow = more sunny days. The white rings mark the target.

m6.title: Moon seasons
m6.intro: Slide through 2030 and see how many sunny days each spot gets every month.
m6.goals: Stars: find a month with no Sun at Malapert · find a month with Sun there · visit all 12 months.
m6.highlight: Malapert gets no Sun at all from January to June 2030 — and again in December.
m6.chartLabel: Malapert sunny days per month in 2030: {list}
m6.why: The Moon’s axis is tilted a tiny bit, so through the year the Sun climbs a little higher or sinks a little lower at the pole. At Malapert, when it sinks, the mountains hide it for months.

m7.title: Ice hunt
m7.intro: Near the pole, some places never see the Sun. They may hold ice! Help Lumi find a safe spot close to the dark.
m7.goals: Stars: 3 for a sunny square next to a dark one, 2 for a sunny square, 1 for trying.
m7.what: Some craters near the pole are so deep that sunlight never reaches their floor. These permanently shadowed places are very cold, so they may hold ice. But they are far too dark and cold for Lumi to land.
m7.pgda: NASA’s long-term map (PGDA) shows that {n} % of the spots within 300 m of Malapert are in permanent shadow.
m7.help: Each square is 100 m. Dark squares had no Sun all of July 2030 (they may get Sun in other months, so they are not the same as permanent shadow). Arrow keys or a tap move the aim; Enter or the button chooses.
m7.mapLabel: Map of sunny days around Malapert in July 2030, 1 km wide, squares of 100 m

result.dark: Too dark! No Sun all of July here, too cold for Lumi to land. Try a sunny square next to it.
result.edge: Great choice! Sunshine for Lumi, right next to a dark area where ice may be.
result.far: Sunny, but far from the dark areas. Try a square right next to one.

m7.none: Pick a square on the map.
m7.legendSun: Lilac to yellow: more sunny days in July 2030
m7.legendDark: Dark blue: no Sun all of July 2030
m7.note: How much ice? Nobody knows yet: there may be some. Scientists are still finding out.

m8.title: Time travel: Apollo 11
m8.intro: Travel back to the Apollo 11 landing site, near the middle of the Moon’s Earth-facing side. Compare its sky with the south pole, over 30 days from 1 July 2030.
m8.goals: Stars: see the Apollo 11 sky · see the Shackleton sky · answer the question.
m8.domeLabel: The sky at {where}: Earth stays between {lo}° and {hi}° above the horizon
m8.apolloText: Apollo 11: Earth stays between {lo}° and {hi}° high, always up in the sky.
m8.shackletonText: Shackleton ridge: Earth goes from {lo}° to {hi}°, so sometimes it is below the horizon.
m8.note: The blue band shows how high Earth goes over the 30 days. 90° is straight up.
m8.question: Where is Earth higher in the sky?
m8.why: At Apollo 11 Earth is about 60° to 70° up. At the south pole it stays near the horizon, so hills can hide it.

m9.title: Final mission: your plan
m9.intro: Choose a spot, a landing date and a battery. Can you find a plan that gets all 3 stars?
m9.sunYes: Sun: {p} % of the time, at least half.
m9.sunNo: Sun: only {p} % of the time. We want at least half.
m9.callYes: Calls: the longest wait without a call is about {n} days, 7 days or less.
m9.callNo: Calls: the longest wait without a call is about {n} days, longer than 7.
m9.callUnknown: Calls: the wait may be even longer than these 30 days can show.
m9.batYes: Battery: Lumi needs {need} kWh for a night of {night}; your {kwh} kWh battery is enough.
m9.batNo: Battery: Lumi needs {need} kWh for a night of {night}; {kwh} kWh is not enough.
m9.batUnknown: Battery: the night may be even longer than these 30 days can show, so we cannot be sure a {kwh} kWh battery is enough (Lumi needs at least {need} kWh for {night}).
m9.rules: How stars are given: the Sun up at least half the time · no more than 7 days without a call · a battery of at least 60 W × the longest night ÷ 0.8.
